html:
A stone gateway of two upright slabs of coral limestone topped by a third, built on the island of Tongatapu in Tonga in the 13th century. It is the best known ancient monument in Polynesia after the moai of Rapa Nui.

Tradition says it was raised by the eleventh Tuʻi Tonga, Tuʻitātui, near his royal seat at Heketā. The name means "the burden of Maui", after the demigod, as if the slabs were the two baskets of a carrying pole. Some say it stood for the king's two sons, a sign that they should live in harmony. In 1967 King Tāufaʻāhau Tupou IV suggested that marks on the top stone line up with sunrise at the solstices, an idea still debated.

It dates from the height of the Tuʻi Tonga line, whose power reached across the seas to Samoa, Fiji and beyond. Moving and setting stones of this size took a ruler who could call on many workers, the same kind of power shown in the great stone tombs of Tonga's chiefs.
